slides.title: Room 7: Past Relationships
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 12. This lesson is about your past relationships. You may listen privately, and you may stop at any time.

slides.quote: “Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. Colossians chapter 3, verses 9 and 10.

“Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.”

slides.title: Not specifically about romance
body: Paul is describing how followers of Jesus live with one another. First a command: “Do not lie to one another.” Then the reason: you have put off the old self and put on the new.
slides.narration: Paul is writing to believers, and this is not specifically about romance. It is about how followers of Jesus live with one another. And notice its shape. It begins with a command: “Do not lie to one another.” Then it gives the reason: you have “put off the old self with its practices” and “put on the new self.”

slides.title: Taking off, putting on
body: The old way of living is set aside. The new self “is being renewed”: a process, not a finished product.
slides.narration: Paul uses a picture of clothing. Taking off one set of clothes, putting on another. The old way of living is set aside. A new way is put on. And notice the new self “is being renewed.” It is a process, not a finished product.

slides.title: Grace does not replace honesty
body: The command to truthfulness, and the fact of renewal. Renewal is what makes honesty possible.
slides.narration:
So two things sit side by side in this passage. The command to truthfulness. And the fact of renewal. Grace does not replace honesty. Renewal is what makes honesty possible.

That is the truth this lesson stands on. Grace does not remove the responsibility to tell consequential truth.

slides.title: New, but not erased
body: Becoming new in Christ does not erase consequences, or the need for honest disclosure. Forgiveness does not require pretending the past did not happen.
slides.narration: The New Testament is clear about grace. In 2 Corinthians 5:17 Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation. Your past does not have to be your identity. But hear the limit of it plainly. Becoming new in Christ does not erase consequences, and it does not remove the need for honest disclosure. Forgiveness does not require pretending the past did not happen. It means the facts do not define who you are.

slides.kicker: One word for each of you
body: To the one disclosing: “God has forgiven me” must never be a reason to withhold what your future spouse reasonably needs. To the one receiving: do not use a disclosure as a weapon.
slides.narration:
So here are two things, one for each of you.

To the person disclosing choices they made: “God has forgiven me” must never become a reason to withhold information your future spouse reasonably needs in order to marry knowingly. Grace received is not a substitute for honesty given.

And to the one receiving it: do not use a disclosure as a weapon. You may still ask relevant questions, need time, or discuss consequences that remain unresolved. Grace does not require an immediate decision, or pretending that every consequence has already been resolved.

slides.kicker: Three ways the past becomes present
chips: The fear that the story repeats
slides.narration: The past becomes present tense very quickly in this room, and it happens in three ways.

slides.title: A competition with someone who is not in the room
body: “Did you love them more than you love me?” The conversation stops being about understanding a history.
slides.narration: The first is comparison. One person discloses something, and the other immediately begins measuring. “Did you love them more than you love me?” “Did you do more for them than for me?” “What did they have that I don’t?” The conversation has stopped being about understanding a history. It has become a competition with someone who is not in the room, and who cannot lose.

slides.kicker: The fear that the story repeats
slides.title: Assessed on what someone else did
body: Ordinary lateness becomes suspicious. Every disagreement carries a second question: is this how it started last time?
slides.narration: The second is the fear that the story repeats. Someone hears about a relationship that ended badly and thinks, “What if I’m next?” Then they start gathering evidence. Ordinary lateness becomes suspicious. Every disagreement carries a second question underneath it: is this how it started last time? The partner is no longer being assessed on who they are. They are being assessed partly on what somebody else did.

slides.title: A wound that predates your partner
body: “The last person left when it got difficult. This one probably will too.”
slides.narration: And the third is quieter: inherited fear in the person who was hurt. “The last person left when it got difficult. This one probably will too.” So they become watchful, or controlling, or endlessly in need of reassurance, not because of anything their partner has done, but because of a wound that predates them.

slides.title: Between two inadequate answers
body: Not “tell everything,” and not “it is under the blood, so do not talk about it.” Your partner deserves the information needed to decide. Not every private detail.
slides.narration: So how much should you tell each other? Two pieces of advice circulate in Christian settings, and neither is adequate. One says, “Tell your partner absolutely everything.” The other says, “Your past is under the blood, so don’t talk about it.” The better principle sits between them. Your partner deserves the information they need to make an informed decision about marrying you. They do not need every private detail of your history.

list: Present legal, financial, parenting or health consequences
A current pattern that may affect faithfulness or safety
Facts that directly change the commitments you ask of your partner
slides.sub: Test: could my partner discover this later and say, “Why didn’t you tell me before we married?”
slides.narration:
So the question is not “What can I possibly confess?” It is: what does this person need to know because it materially affects our marriage? Material information includes present legal, financial, parenting or health consequences; ongoing contact or obligations; a current pattern that may affect faithfulness or safety; and facts that directly change the commitments you are asking your partner to make. Here is a helpful test: is there anything material, in that sense, that my partner could discover later that would lead them to say, “Why didn’t you tell me before we married?”

Examples of material information include a previous marriage, an existing child, continuing legal or financial obligations, relevant health consequences, ongoing contact, or a current pattern that could affect faithfulness or safety.

slides.title: Your choices, and harm done to you
body: Take responsibility for your own choices. But abuse, coercion or betrayal committed against you is not your sin to confess. You control whether, when and how you tell that story.
slides.narration: But hear a distinction first. There is a difference between actions you chose and harm done to you. Take responsibility for your own choices. But abuse, coercion or betrayal committed against you is not your sin to confess. You control whether, when and how you tell the story of what happened. If it has a present consequence that directly affects your partner’s health, safety or shared commitments, make a safe plan to disclose that consequence without being required to narrate the experience. An experience of abuse does not become a debt of detailed disclosure simply because someone else wants to know.

slides.title: Is there anything material that my partner could discover later and reasonably ask why I hadn’t told them?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. Is there anything material that my partner could discover later and reasonably ask why I hadn’t told them? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: Truthful without being graphic
body: “There are choices in my past I am not proud of, and I want you to know what is relevant before we marry.” Do not conceal significant history or ongoing consequences.
slides.narration: Sexual history needs particular care. Honesty does not require exchanging a detailed catalogue of previous experiences. That produces mental images, comparison and jealousy without producing anything useful. But nor should anyone conceal significant history, ongoing consequences or anything that will directly affect the marriage simply because it happened before. You can be truthful without being graphic. When disclosing choices you made, you might say: “There are choices in my past I am not proud of, and I want you to know what is relevant before we marry. I’ll answer reasonable questions, but I don’t think describing every detail would help either of us.” That is honest. It is not an interrogation.

slides.title: Vulnerability should serve truth
body: Do not disclose something painful to test whether your partner will prove their love by how they receive it.
slides.narration: And do not disclose something painful as a test of whether your partner will prove their love by how they receive it. Vulnerability should serve truth, preparation and trust. It should not be used as an examination.

slides.title: Not yours to carry
body: Reflect on your own choices, but do not take responsibility for another person’s abuse or betrayal.
slides.narration: If you are the one who has been hurt, please hear this. Reflect on your own choices, but do not take responsibility for another person’s abuse or betrayal. What matters is whether each of you can describe relevant experiences honestly and take responsibility for your own behaviour.

body: Hearing: “What exactly am I afraid of?” Disclosing: “Am I telling this because my partner needs to know, or because I need them to carry my guilt?”
slides.narration: To the one hearing a disclosure, ask yourself: “What exactly am I afraid of?” Push past the first answer. The fear may include thoughts such as, “I am not enough,” or, “What if this happens to me?” Those may be the actual wounds, and they can be addressed. Repeatedly examining more details rarely resolves those fears and may deepen comparison. To the one disclosing, ask: “Am I telling this because my partner needs to know, or because I need them to carry my guilt?” Your future spouse may offer care and grace, but neither person can be solely responsible for the other’s recovery.

slides.title: About twenty minutes
list: Is there anything in my past that could materially affect this marriage?
Is there anything my partner could discover later and reasonably ask why I hadn’t told them?
Is there anything I am hoping never comes up?
slides.narration:
Your step has two parts. First, about twenty minutes alone. Is there anything in my past that could materially affect this marriage? Is there anything my partner could discover later and reasonably ask why I hadn’t told them? Is there anything I am hoping never comes up? Your written answers remain private. If they reveal information that materially affects the marriage, make a safe plan to disclose that information before proceeding with the wedding. You still control unnecessary details.

Take responsibility for choices you made. Harm done to you is not your sin to confess, and you control the details of that story.

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes, in private
body: Either of you may stop at any time. Share only what is needed. The receiver may ask what they need to know to decide, not detail whose only function is to picture it.
slides.narration: Then set aside 45 to 60 minutes, in a private place, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Either of you may stop at any time. Work through three main questions. First: is there anything material my partner needs to know in order to decide, or do I have nothing material to add? Share only what is needed. The one receiving it uses what we learned in Lesson 5: a question first, repeat it back, then respond. And here is a rule for this conversation: the receiver may ask what they need to know in order to decide. They may not ask for detail whose only function is to picture it. If you are not sure which you are asking for, ask yourself what you would do with the answer.

slides.kicker: How the past shows up in the present
body: Do I compare you to anyone? What makes me jealous, and what fear sits underneath? Am I hiding any present contact that crosses a boundary we agreed?
slides.narration: Second: how does the past show up in the present? Do I compare you to anyone? What makes me jealous, and what fear sits underneath that jealousy? Am I still in contact with anyone from my past? Is there any present contact I am hiding because I know it crosses a boundary we have agreed? That last one is a question to ask yourself honestly, not a demand to hand over a phone.

body: With what I now know, am I able to continue discerning this marriage freely, and to respond without shaming, threatening or retaliating? Do I need more time?
slides.narration: And third, the closing question, out loud, from both of you: with what I now know, am I able to continue discerning this marriage freely, and to respond without shaming, threatening or retaliating? Do I need more time, information or support before answering? Do not answer quickly. If the honest answer is “I need time,” take the time. That is a far better answer than a yes you cannot keep.

slides.kicker: If a joint conversation would not be safe
slides.note: Do not force a disclosure if doing so could put you at risk. Do not hold the conversation. Make a confidential plan with a qualified support person instead.
slides.narration: Do not force a disclosure in this exercise if doing so could put you at risk. If a joint conversation would not be safe, do not hold it. Make a confidential plan with a qualified support person instead. Record only the next steps you both agree are useful. You do not need a written catalogue of private history.

body: Lord, thank You that You forgive, and that You are renewing us. Give us courage to tell the truth that matters, and wisdom to leave unsaid what only wounds. Where we carry shame, lift it. Where we carry fear, quiet it. Help us receive one another with grace, without pretending, and without punishing. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, thank You that You forgive, and that You are renewing us. Give us courage to tell the truth that matters, and wisdom to leave unsaid what only wounds. Where we carry shame, lift it. Where we carry fear, quiet it. Help us receive one another with grace, without pretending, and without punishing. Amen.
